concepts.definition: When an event happens, the processor leaves what it is doing, runs the matching function, and then goes back to where it left off.
concepts.example: When the button on D2 drops to LOW, the function basildi() runs, whatever loop() is doing.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking an interrupt solves every problem; long jobs cannot be done inside an ISR.

concepts.definition: Interrupt service routine: a short function that runs when an interrupt arrives, takes no parameters and returns no value.
concepts.example: The function void basildi() { sayac++; } is an ISR.
concepts.pitfall: Putting delay or Serial.print inside an ISR; the program may get stuck.

concepts.definition: A keyword that tells the compiler a variable can change outside the normal flow of the program (in an ISR).
concepts.pitfall: Not writing volatile: loop() may read the value from an old copy and the counter seems not to go up.

concepts.definition: The setting that decides which event triggers attachInterrupt: FALLING, RISING, CHANGE, LOW.
concepts.example: FALLING is used to catch a press on an INPUT_PULLUP button.
concepts.pitfall: Choosing CHANGE and thinking one press is one interrupt; a press and a release produce two interrupts.

concepts.definition: A regular interrupt produced when one of the counters in the board's timer units reaches a set value.
concepts.example: With prescaler 256 and OCR1A = 31249, the interrupt comes every 0.5 seconds.
concepts.pitfall: Using Timer1 together with Servo or with analogWrite on pins 9-10: the same unit clashes.

quiz.prompt: On the Arduino Uno, which pins can take an external interrupt with attachInterrupt?
quiz.explanation: On the Uno, external interrupts are only on the INT0 (D2) and INT1 (D3) pins. D0 and D1 are for serial communication; D8-D9 and the other pins do not have this interrupt.

quiz.prompt: Timer1 is running with prescaler 256 (16 MHz / 256 = 62 500 ticks/s) and OCR1A = 6249 has been written. Every how many milliseconds does the interrupt come?
quiz.explanation: The number of ticks counted is OCR1A + 1 = 6250. 6250 / 62 500 = 0.1 s = 100 ms. If you forget the +1 and work out 6249 / 62 500, you get 99.98 ms; the right formula uses (OCR1A + 1).

options: On the Uno, D4 is not an external interrupt pin; the interrupt must be set up on D2 or D3
The say() function should be volatile
HIGH should be written instead of FALLING
The basis variable should not be unsigned
quiz.explanation: On the Uno, external interrupts exist only on pins D2 (INT0) and D3 (INT1); digitalPinToInterrupt(4) does not give a valid interrupt number, so attachInterrupt sets nothing up. The button must be moved to D2. say() is an ISR; volatile is written for variables; FALLING is the right mode; being unsigned is not a problem.

options: Nothing is printed, the program gets stuck
quiz.explanation: CHANGE produces an interrupt for both the press (HIGH→LOW) and the release (LOW→HIGH); two interrupts make the counter 2. If FALLING had been chosen, the result would be 1. The interrupt works even inside delay, so it is not 0 and the program does not get stuck.

quiz.prompt: Why is it not a good idea to use Serial.println inside an interrupt function?
options: Printing is slow and the program may get stuck if the buffer fills up; an ISR must be short
No variables can be used inside an ISR
The Serial monitor turns interrupts off
quiz.explanation: An ISR must be short. Serial.println is slow, and it may have to wait if the output buffer fills up; inside an interrupt, the interrupts that would let that wait finish are turned off. Raising a flag and leaving the printing to loop() is right. Variables can be used in an ISR (they need to be volatile).
